I've been farming this land in Quzhou for 37 years. I know the soil here — the sandy loam in my fields drains fast but heats up early in spring. With well irrigation I'm not dependent on rainfall, which matters because summers can be unpredictable.

My 12 mu splits naturally: 6 mu stays in the wheat-maize rotation — that's my anchor, reliable income and food security. The other 6 mu I divide between cotton (4 mu) and chili (2 mu). Cotton has been part of this area's farming culture and I know how to manage it, though pest pressure is serious. Chili is labor-intensive but the value per mu is high, and with only two of us in the household I won't push it beyond 2 mu.

For wheat I use a certified improved variety — Jimai 22 performs consistently here. I apply nitrogen in two splits: base fertilizer before sowing, then topdress at jointing. Three irrigations: winter water before freeze, jointing, and heading. Two pesticide passes — one herbicide in winter, one for aphids and rust in spring.

Summer maize I plant straight after wheat harvest, no-till is tempting but I do rotary to break up the straw. Hybrid seed only — I haven't used open-pollinated maize in 20 years. Summer rains do some work so I only irrigate twice: at tasseling and grain fill.

Cotton gets the most attention. Six pest applications — bollworm and whitefly don't forgive neglect. I deep plough this field in spring to break the hardpan. Five irrigations through the long season.

Chili is transplanted in late April. I ridge-plant and irrigate from the well frequently because this crop responds to moisture but also rots fast if drainage is poor. Four pesticide passes for aphids, mites, and anthracnose.
